message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Dominated by the most common isotope, protium (¹H). |
| **Isotopes** | ¹H (protium, 99.98 %), ²H (deuterium, 0.02 %), ³H (tritium, trace, radioactive). | Deuterium and tritium are used in nuclear fusion research. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron → highly reactive. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Highest of all elements. |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | Negative value indicates energy release when an electron is added. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low; hydrogen is a gas at room temperature. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Solidifies only at cryogenic temperatures. |
| **Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ | Less dense than air; rises to the sky. |
| **Molar volume (ideal gas)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard at 0 °C, 1 atm. |
| **Solubility in water** | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 20 °C | Low, but increases with pressure. |
| **Reactivity** | Extremely reactive; forms hydrides (e.g., NaH, CaH₂) and covalent bonds (e.g., H₂O, CH₄). | Forms a wide range of compounds; key in organic chemistry. |
| **Flammability** | Highly flammable; explosive mixture with air (4–75 % H₂). | Used as rocket fuel (liquid hydrogen). |
| **Bonding** | Forms single covalent bonds; diatomic H₂ is the most stable form. | Can form H⁺ (proton) in acid–base chemistry. |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series (UV, visible, IR). | Basis for astronomical hydrogen detection. |
| **Magnetic moment** | 2.792847 µB (electron spin) | Proton has a magnetic moment of 2.792847 µB. |
| **Heat capacity (gas)** | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 298 K) | Low due to light mass. |
| **Thermal conductivity** | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 300 K) | High relative to other gases. |
| **Electrical conductivity** | Very low in neutral state; becomes high when ionized (plasma). | Used in plasma physics and fusion research. |
| **Phase diagram** | Triple point at 13.99 K, 0.006 atm; critical point at 33.19 K, 1.3 atm. | Shows hydrogen’s unique phase behavior. |

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Only one proton and one electron.
- **Highly reactive**: Forms a vast array of compounds; key in both inorganic and organic chemistry.
- **Low boiling/melting points**: Exists as a gas under normal conditions; requires cryogenic temperatures to liquefy or solidify.
- **Flammable & explosive**: Must be handled with care; used as rocket fuel and in industrial processes.
- **Isotopic significance**: Deuterium and tritium are crucial for nuclear fusion and tracer studies.
- **Spectroscopic importance**: Hydrogen lines are fundamental in astrophysics for identifying stellar compositions.

These properties make hydrogen a cornerstone of chemistry, physics, and engineering, from everyday fuels to cutting‑edge fusion research.
